clinician.final_diagnosis: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus) empyema necessitans in an adult male
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 61-year-old male with history of throat cancer s/p chemo-radiation, SIADH, GERD, and former smoking presented with acute hematemesis, sharp burning epigastric pain, nausea, one week of right shoulder pain, and two days of right anterior chest fullness. Initial portable chest X-ray on admission was unremarkable (no focal airspace opacities or pleural effusions). Contrast-enhanced CT chest revealed a 6.5×3.8 cm complex right pleural space collection with air foci within the right pectoral muscles, consistent with empyema necessitans (spontaneous rupture of empyema through the chest wall). CT-guided drainage by interventional radiology yielded 15 cc of purulent material with placement of a 12 French pigtail catheter. Culture of the abscess grew Group B Streptococcus (GBS); pathology showed bacteria with no fungal growth and no malignant cells; AFB smear was negative. Laboratory data on admission showed leukocytosis (WBC 17.8 with 90% neutrophils) and hyponatremia (sodium 115 mEq). The patient was initially treated with Piperacillin-Tazobactam and switched to Ampicillin/Sulbactam based on antibiotic sensitivities. Thoracic surgery consultation was requested with initial plan for surgical intervention, but the patient self-removed the drain and declined surgery. After multidisciplinary discussion involving infectious disease, pulmonology, and thoracic surgery, medical management was continued. Chest radiograph at six months after discharge showed complete resolution of the infection.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: 61-year-old male presenting with acute hematemesis and epigastric pain
One week of right shoulder pain and two days of right anterior chest fullness preceding hematemesis
Initial portable chest X-ray on admission showed no focal airspace opacities or pleural effusions
CT chest revealed 6.5×3.8 cm complex right pleural space collection with air foci within right pectoral muscles
CT-guided drainage performed by interventional radiology with 15 cc purulent material removed and 12 French pigtail catheter placed
Pleural fluid/abscess culture grew Group B Streptococcus (GBS)
Pathology showed bacteria, no fungal growth, no malignant cells, and AFB smear negative
Laboratory data on admission: leukocytosis (WBC 17.8 with 90% neutrophils) and hyponatremia (sodium 115 mEq)
Initial antibiotic therapy with Piperacillin-Tazobactam, switched to Ampicillin/Sulbactam based on sensitivities
Thoracic surgery consultation requested; patient self-removed drain and declined surgery
Chest radiograph at six months after discharge showed resolution of infection

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.alternative: Primary esophageal or gastric pathology (peptic ulcer disease, esophageal rupture)
ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: CT imaging showed pleural collection with chest wall involvement rather than primary GI pathology; hematemesis explained by erosion of infected pleural collection into GI tract
Pathology showed no fungal growth and AFB smear was negative
CT-guided drainage yielded purulent material with positive bacterial culture, confirming empyema
